slot.brief: Evaluate a definite integral of a rational function of sin x (and cos x) over [0, π] or [0, π/2] using t = tan(x/2) substitution; answer a clean closed form.

verdicts.working: With t = tan(x/2), the limits are 0 to ∞ and the integral becomes 2∫₀^∞ dt/[(t²+1)(t²+t+1)]. Using partial fractions, its antiderivative is ln[(t²+t+1)/(t²+1)] + ∫dt/(t²+t+1). The logarithmic term vanishes at both limits, and the remaining integral is 2π/(3√3).

working:
$t=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$ gives $I=2\int_0^\infty\dfrac{dt}{(1+t^2)(t^2+t+1)}$; $\dfrac{1}{(1+t^2)(t^2+t+1)}=-\dfrac{t}{1+t^2}+\dfrac{t+1}{t^2+t+1}$. Thus $I=\left[\ln\dfrac{t^2+t+1}{1+t^2}\right]_0^\infty+\int_0^\infty\dfrac{dt}{t^2+t+1}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}$.

Independent check: With t = tan(x/2), the limits are 0 to ∞ and the integral becomes 2∫₀^∞ dt/[(t²+1)(t²+t+1)]. Using partial fractions, its antiderivative is ln[(t²+t+1)/(t²+1)] + ∫dt/(t²+t+1). The logarithmic term vanishes at both limits, and the remaining integral is 2π/(3√3).
solution:
Using $t=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$, we have $\sin x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $1+\cos x=\dfrac{2}{1+t^2}$, and $dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$.
$$I=2\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{(1+t^2)(t^2+t+1)}$$
Since $\dfrac{1}{(1+t^2)(t^2+t+1)}=-\dfrac{t}{1+t^2}+\dfrac{t+1}{t^2+t+1}$, the logarithmic boundary term vanishes, giving $I=\int_0^\infty\dfrac{dt}{t^2+t+1}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}$.
